query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An advanced machine‐learning (ML) potential framework, trained on a minimal but representative set of ab initio molecular dynamics data from both the solid and liquid phases near fusion conditions, can be used to conduct ML-accelerated thermodynamic integration that reproduces the full free-energy landscape (including vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions) at a significantly reduced computational cost compared to explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD workflows.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high‐entropy alloys (e.g., a prototypical CoCrFeMnNi alloy) near their fusion (melting) conditions with both chemically disordered solid and liquid phases.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy an ML potential framework which is calibrated from a limited set of high-temperature ab initio MD simulations sampling both solid and liquid configurations. Then, use this ML potential within an enhanced free-energy sampling (thermodynamic integration) protocol to compute phase free energies.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions near the fusion transition for multicomponent high-entropy systems, ensuring that both the solid and liquid phase configurations (and their associated entropy contributions) are well represented.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential acts as the mediator by accurately interpolating the potential energy surface with retention of vibrational entropy, anharmonic effects, and electron–vibration coupling, even in the complex configurational space of high-entropy alloys.
generation.mechanism: By training on targeted ab initio MD data in both phases, the ML potential learns to predict energies and forces with near first-principles accuracy. This allows the subsequent thermodynamic integration to capture free-energy differences without the prohibitive cost of full MD, while maintaining the fidelity of key entropy contributions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Free-energy differences (and derived properties such as the fusion temperature and entropy contributions) will be obtained with an error margin that is comparable to explicit ab initio MD (e.g., on the order of a few meV/atom) while achieving a computational speedup likely by one to two orders of magnitude relative to explicit MD and improved scalability over TOR-TILD in multicomponent systems.
generation.baseline: Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy evaluations that fully capture vibrational and electron–vibration effects at a high computational cost.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be valid for multicomponent high-entropy alloy systems near their melting temperatures where both solid and liquid free energies are required. Its applicability may be limited if the configurational space extends beyond what is sampled in the limited ab initio training set.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding whether the trained ML potential can adequately extrapolate to rare or subtle configurational states that significantly contribute to the entropy, potentially impacting the accuracy of free-energy differences in very complex multicomponent systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform independent explicit ab initio molecular dynamics free-energy calculations for both the solid and liquid phases of the selected CoCrFeMnNi alloy near its fusion transition. In parallel, use the ML potential–driven thermodynamic integration method to compute the phase free energies. Compare the free-energy differences, fusion temperature predictions, and vibrational/anharmonic entropy contributions between the two approaches.
measurements: Absolute free energies per atom for both phases
Fusion (melting) temperature and associated phase transition parameters
Quantitative assessments of vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration entropy contributions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the ML-accelerated method yields phase free energies or derived observables (e.g., fusion temperature or entropy contributions) with discrepancies consistently exceeding a predefined error threshold (e.g., >5 meV/atom error or >5% deviation in fusion temperature) compared to the explicit ab initio MD results, or if the method fails to capture critical features (such as anharmonicity) present in the ab initio data.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. decision.trend: The field has evolved from extremely costly explicit ab initio molecular dynamics—capable of reproducing all vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration coupling effects—with direct free-energy evaluations, to schemes such as TOR-TILD that improved throughput for elemental and binary systems. However, when applied to multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their fusion transitions, these methods face significant scaling challenges while still demanding full phase free-energy fidelity. In essence, what was tried so far either sacrifices cost for accuracy or becomes prohibitively slow when complexity increases, leaving the dual-phase, high-temperature free-energy evaluation problem unresolved.
decision.unsolved: There is no cost‐effective method that can accurately capture the free energies (including all vibrational entropy, anharmonic corrections, and electron–vibration coupling) of both solid and liquid phases in multicomponent high‐entropy systems near fusion. The challenge is to extend the accuracy of first‐principles dynamics while avoiding the computational expense of explicit MD and the slowdown of existing accelerated methods like TOR-TILD.
decision.lever: Develop an advanced machine learning (ML) potential framework—trained via a minimal set of ab initio MD and free-energy data that includes both the solid and liquid phases at high temperatures—to drive an enhanced free-energy sampling scheme (e.g., ML-accelerated thermodynamic integration).
decision.why: Recent advances in ML potentials have demonstrated that they can faithfully reproduce complex phase behaviors and thermodynamic properties in both elemental and binary systems while offering orders-of-magnitude computational speedup. This evolution naturally suggests that, for complex multicomponent high-entropy systems, an ML-based approach can inherit the fidelity of explicit ab initio calculations yet bypass the cost and scaling limitations of traditional MD or TOR-TILD. A decisive benchmark would be that the phase free energies and derived observables (e.g., fusion temperature shifts, entropy contributions) computed with the ML method fall within a narrow error margin relative to a subset of explicit ab initio MD results across the targeted compositional space and temperature regime.
